answer.answer: Gross margin doesn't apply to JPMorgan Chase. JPM is a bank holding company, and its income statement has no cost of goods sold and no gross profit line, so the gross-margin consistency test can't be run. Its revenue is reported as net interest income (interest earned minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings) plus noninterest revenue (fees, trading and similar income). Its profitability is judged with bank measures such as net interest income, net yield on interest-earning assets, efficiency ratio, return on tangible common equity and credit costs. These can swing a lot with interest rates: for example, net interest income rose 49% year over year, from $13,872 million in Q1 2022 to $20,711 million in Q1 2023.

answer.answer: Verizon's FY2022 quick ratio is about 0.54x (cash $2,605M plus net receivables $24,506M, against current liabilities of $50,171M). It has only about 54 cents of quick assets for each dollar of short-term obligations, so on this measure alone it looks weak, below the usual 1.0x benchmark. The ratio is still relevant, but it is a limited test for a large telecom like Verizon: steady subscription revenue and cash from operations, plus access to financing, pay its short-term bills rather than cash on hand, so a low quick ratio is normal for the industry and does not by itself point to a liquidity problem.

answer.answer: Gross margin isn't a useful measure for American Express. It is a card issuer, payments network and bank, so its income statement has no cost of goods sold and no gross profit line; the top line is 'total revenues net of interest expense' ($52,862M in FY2022, up 25% from $42,380M), followed by credit-loss provisions and operating expenses such as Card Member rewards. Better measures are net interest income and net interest yield, the provision for credit losses, the expense mix and pretax margin. On that basis, pretax margin fell from about 25.2% in FY2021 to 18.1% in FY2022: revenue grew on 23% higher billed business (discount revenue up 25%), premium card fee growth (net card fees up 17%) and net interest income up 28% from larger loan balances and higher rates, but credit-loss provisions swung from a $1,419M release to a $2,182M charge, and Card Member rewards (+$2,995M), business development, Card Member services and other expenses rose.
answer.calculation: Pretax margin (in place of gross margin) = pretax income / total revenues net of interest expense. FY2022: 9,585 / 52,862 = 18.1%. FY2021: 10,689 / 42,380 = 25.2%.

answer.answer: Operating margin isn't a useful metric for American Express. It is a bank holding company and card issuer: interest expense is part of its cost of revenue, so it reports 'total revenues net of interest expense', and provisions for credit losses swing earnings. Its income statement has no operating income line. The closest measure, pretax margin (pretax income ÷ revenues net of interest expense), was 11.9% in 2020, 25.2% in 2021 and 18.1% in 2022, so it fell in 2022 rather than improving. Most of that swing comes from credit loss provisions (a $1.4B release in 2021 versus a $2.2B charge in 2022); before provisions, the margin was roughly flat at 21.9% in 2021 and 22.3% in 2022, still below 25.0% in 2020.
answer.calculation: Pretax margin = pretax income / total revenues net of interest expense: 2022 9,585/52,862 = 18.13%; 2021 10,689/42,380 = 25.22%; 2020 4,296/36,087 = 11.90%. Pre-provision margin = (pretax income + provisions for credit losses) / revenues net of interest expense: 2022 (9,585+2,182)/52,862 = 22.26%; 2021 (10,689−1,419)/42,380 = 21.87%; 2020 (4,296+4,730)/36,087 = 25.01%.

answer.answer: At the end of Q2 FY2023 (December 31, 2022), Amcor had a restructuring plan liability of $93 million, down from $118 million at June 30, 2022. It was made up of $81 million in employee costs such as severance, $2 million in fixed-asset-related costs and $10 million in other costs, such as facility exit costs. These were accrued costs for exit and restructuring actions not yet paid, mainly for the response to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the sale of Amcor's Russian business, mostly in the Flexibles segment, with some carry-over from the largely completed 2019 Bemis integration plan. The purpose was to reduce structural costs (the FY2023 10-K says Amcor expects about $50 million a year in pre-tax savings by FY2025 from all its Russia-related restructuring); Amcor expected to pay most of the liability within 12 months and recorded it under other current and other non-current liabilities.
answer.calculation: Movement from June 30, 2022 to December 31, 2022 ($ millions): 118 opening balance + 2 net charges - 25 cash paid - 2 reversal of unused amounts = 93 closing balance. By type: 81 employee + 2 fixed-asset-related + 10 other = 93.

answer.answer: Walmart's average unadjusted EBITDA margin for FY2018–FY2020 was about 6.2%. By year it was 6.19% in FY2018, 6.34% in FY2019 and 6.02% in FY2020. EBITDA here is operating income plus depreciation and amortization from the cash flow statement, divided by total revenues.
answer.calculation: Each year's EBITDA margin is (operating income + D&A) / total revenues; the result is the simple average of the three years' margins. All figures are in $ millions.
